clue.text: Composer seen to be rich icon

indicators.note: something seen to has been fixed or worked over, so the following words are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a composer is apparently a wealthy idol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen to' reads as part of 'seen to be', but it is the anagram signal: BE RICH ICON is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi Boccherini was an eighteenth-century Italian cellist and writer of chamber music.

clue.text: Emily Dickinson's confiding prodigal

parts.note: a phrase lifted from a Dickinson poem, where the 'confiding prodigal' is a golden songbird touched by Midas

explanation.surface: A trusting spendthrift from the poems of Emily Dickinson.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickinson's poem 'One of the ones that Midas touched' calls this bird 'that confiding prodigal'; the clue is pure literary knowledge, with no count printed.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem names the songbird it describes as 'the blissful' one of that species.

clue.text: Lamb on a string for loving daughter

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece placed on another comes first, above it

parts.note: a cord is a length of string
Charles Lamb wrote his essays under the pen name Elia

explanation.surface: A young sheep kept on a leash is a present for a devoted girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb' looks like the animal but is the essayist Charles Lamb, whose pen name was Elia. The answer is King Lear's faithful youngest child.
explanation.definitionFit: In King Lear she is the youngest child, the one who truly loves her father though she will not flatter him.

clue.text: Divine messenger slips through damaged sieve to spread the Gospel Part of church where we may bring forth creativity

indicators.note: the messenger passes into the middle of the broken sieve, so one piece sits inside the other
a damaged sieve is knocked out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: an angel is a messenger of God

explanation.surface: A heavenly envoy squeezes through a broken strainer on a preaching mission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' turns SIEVE into EVISE; 'slips through' puts ANGEL inside it, EV-ANGEL-ISE. The held text runs on into the next clue's words, which belong to INSPIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: To evangelise is to preach Christianity and win converts.

clue.text: Part of church where we may bring forth creativity

definitions.text: Part of church where we may bring forth creativity

parts.words: Part of church where we may bring forth creativity
parts.note: split as two words, the answer says 'in the tall pointed top of a church'; whole, it means to stir creative thought

explanation.surface: A corner of the church building where ideas are born.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words the answer is IN SPIRE, the place in a church; read whole it means to fill someone with creative energy.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspire is to rouse someone to produce new ideas or art.

clue.text: Collingwood certainly had some of history

definitions.text: Collingwood certainly had some of history

parts.words: Collingwood certainly had some of history
parts.note: R. G. Collingwood, the Oxford philosopher, wrote a famous book of historical theory, so he had a notion 'of History'

explanation.surface: The historian Collingwood plainly knew a bit about the past.
explanation.walkthrough: R. G. Collingwood's best-known book is 'The Idea of History' (1946); 'had some of history' means had that notion of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The book title pairs a notion or concept with history, so Collingwood certainly had one.

clue.text: Patterns may be formed by this architectural feature

indicators.note: the clue says the word may be made by reworking the letters of its neighbour, a sign that they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Decorative designs might be created by some part of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests tracery patterns made by a building; the letters of PATTERNS rearranged make the church's cross arm.
explanation.definitionFit: A transept is either arm of the cross-shaped plan of a church, an architectural element.

clue.text: Characteristic of Carpenter protagonist, bringing final despair to Echo

definitions.text: Characteristic of Carpenter protagonist, bringing final despair to Echo

parts.words: Characteristic of Carpenter protagonist, bringing final despair to Echo
parts.note: Edward Carpenter wrote poems on the youth of Greek myth who loved his own reflection and spurned the nymph Echo

explanation.surface: A trait of the hero of Carpenter's verse drove Echo to despair.
explanation.walkthrough: In the myth the nymph Echo pines away because the beautiful youth loves only his own image; Edward Carpenter's 'Narcissus and Other Poems' (1873) has him as its hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive self-love is the trait named after the youth of Greek myth who fell for his reflection.

clue.text: Kerouac tramps

parts.note: tramps are bums, and Jack Kerouac's 1958 novel is 'The ___ Bums'

explanation.surface: Wanderers in the writing of Jack Kerouac.
explanation.walkthrough: Kerouac's novel 'The Dharma Bums' supplies the word: tramps are bums, so Kerouac's tramps are the Dharma Bums.
explanation.definitionFit: The Buddhist and Hindu term for cosmic law and duty gives the title of Kerouac's novel about wandering seekers.

clue.text: It seems it's Dora Saint's work which girl studies mistakenly

definitions.text: It seems it's Dora Saint's work which girl studies mistakenly

parts.words: It seems it's Dora Saint's work which girl studies mistakenly
parts.note: Dora Saint wrote village novels as 'Miss Read', so her books are Miss Read's; a girl (miss) who reads makes the same sound, and the word means takes the wrong sense

explanation.surface: Seemingly a schoolgirl's set texts are the novels of Dora Saint.
explanation.walkthrough: Dora Saint's pen name was Miss Read, so 'Dora Saint's work' sounds like Miss Read's; with one S the word means studies mistakenly.
explanation.definitionFit: To misread is to interpret a text or situation wrongly.

clue.text: Philosopher's view of strange peak bracer

indicators.note: a strange peak is an odd version of the word, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: an alp is a high mountain peak
a tonic is a drink that braces or invigorates

explanation.surface: A thinker considers an odd mountain a pick-me-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges ALP into PLA; TONIC follows. 'view of' joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Platonic means relating to Plato, the Greek thinker.

clue.text: Protective covering much appreciated by Jim Dixon

definitions.meaning: the rind or skin of fruit that protects it
said ironically: in Kingsley Amis's Lucky Jim, Dixon's clinging colleague Margaret has this surname and he dreads her

explanation.surface: Jim Dixon is fond of a protective layer.
explanation.walkthrough: Jim Dixon is the hero of Kingsley Amis's novel Lucky Jim; 'much appreciated' is ironic, since he longs to escape Margaret Peel.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit rind shields the flesh; and Margaret, the neurotic lecturer in Lucky Jim, shares the surname.

clue.text: Universal language may put all in the picture

definitions.text: Universal language may put all in the picture

parts.words: Universal language may put all in the picture
parts.note: a proposed script of symbols readable in any tongue; its Greek roots mean 'all' and 'writing', so it puts everyone in the picture

explanation.surface: A language everyone understands could tell everyone what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is built from Greek pasi 'for all' and graphia 'writing'; 'put all in the picture' plays on informing everyone and on writing in pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasigraphy is a system of written symbols meant to be understood by speakers of every language.

clue.text: Unhappy Lear gets flowers from author of Cordial

indicators.note: an unhappy Lear is upset, so his letters are disturbed

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river

explanation.surface: Miserable King Lear receives a bouquet from a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowers' means things that flow, rivers, not blooms. Anthony Woodville, Earl Rivers, translated 'Cordiale', printed by Caxton in 1479.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Woodville, brother-in-law of Edward IV, translated the devotional work 'Cordiale'.

clue.text: Lector on liner shows a measure of interest

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece placed on another stands above it

parts.note: a lector is one who reads, especially aloud in church or as a university lecturer
an ocean liner is a passenger ship

explanation.surface: A reader travelling on a cruise boat displays some curiosity.
explanation.walkthrough: A paper's readership measures how many people take an interest in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Readership counts the audience of a publication, gauging how much interest it attracts.

clue.text: Diabolic novel verses

explanation.surface: A wicked book of poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Salman Rushdie's novel 'The Satanic Verses' (1988) supplies the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish means relating to the Devil; and Rushdie's 1988 novel title is The Satanic Verses.

clue.text: Big girl from Uranus

parts.note: in Greek myth Uranus, the sky, fathered a race of giants on Gaia; his giant daughters are female members of that race

explanation.surface: A large young woman from the seventh planet.
explanation.walkthrough: Uranus here is the sky god of Greek myth, not the planet; his children were the giant Titans, and a female one is this.
explanation.definitionFit: A female Titan, one of the giant children of the sky god and the earth goddess.

clue.text: Indian language from Colmar, a think ing man's means of communication

indicators.note: the language is taken out of the run of words that follows, a sign of letters lifted from inside them

explanation.surface: A regional tongue spoken by a philosopher in the Alsatian town of Colmar.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through 'ColMAR A THInk'. The held text splits 'thinking' as 'think ing', an OCR break; the hidden run needs only 'think'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marathi is the main language of the Indian state of Maharashtra.

clue.text: Berta Ruck's dreadful girl

parts.note: Berta Ruck, Welsh romantic novelist, wrote a book about an awful young heroine

explanation.surface: A frightful young woman from the novels of Berta Ruck.
explanation.walkthrough: Berta Ruck's novel 'Arabella the Awful' (1918) gives the dreadful girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Berta Ruck's 'the Awful' novel bears this name.

clue.text: Novelist no doubt calm, following storm

definitions.text: Novelist no doubt calm, following storm

parts.words: Novelist no doubt calm, following storm
parts.note: the Yorkshire novelist Margaret Storm ___ had 'Storm' before her surname, so her surname follows a storm

explanation.surface: A writer is surely serene after the tempest has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist is Storm Jameson (1891-1986); her surname literally follows 'Storm', and the calm after a storm is proverbial.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Storm Jameson was a prolific English novelist known by the name Storm Jameson.

clue.text: "He'd — so fast it would make his head swim" (Sinclair Lewis, Babbitt)

definitions.text: "He'd — so fast it would make his head swim" (Sinclair Lewis, Babbitt)

parts.words: "He'd — so fast it would make his head swim" (Sinclair Lewis, Babbitt)
parts.note: the missing words from the quotation are an American idiom for being sacked

explanation.surface: A line from Sinclair Lewis's novel Babbitt with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in the quotation: to be dismissed abruptly is, in American slang, to be shown the door.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for being dismissed from a job or sent away.

clue.text: Bulwer-Lytton's schoolmaster, an artist in the morning

indicators.note: the artist is placed within the morning, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: AM stands for ante meridiem, before noon
RA is a Royal Academician, a recognised artist

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist's teacher turns out to be a painter at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts RA inside AM. Bulwer-Lytton's novel 'Eugene Aram' (1832) is about a schoolmaster who was a murderer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Aram, the scholarly teacher hanged for murder, is the title figure of Bulwer-Lytton's novel.

clue.text: Some articles on north-eastern goddess

indicators.note: in a down clue the articles placed on top of the next piece come first

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
the is the definite article
NE is the abbreviation for north-east

explanation.surface: A few pieces of writing about a deity from the north-east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' gives both A and THE, the indefinite and definite articles, not pieces of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Athene is the Greek deity of wisdom, patron of Athens.

clue.text: Add glosses for article on new (and old) gallery

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: Write captions for a report about a gallery, both modern and historic.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the Tate's new and old buildings (Tate Modern and Tate Britain), but 'new' and 'old' are just N and O.
explanation.definitionFit: To annotate is to supply explanatory notes on a text.

clue.text: Valiant as the lion, churlish as the bear, in Alexander's opinion

definitions.text: Valiant as the lion, churlish as the bear, in Alexander's opinion

parts.words: Valiant as the lion, churlish as the bear, in Alexander's opinion
parts.note: in Troilus and Cressida, Cressida's servant Alexander describes a Greek warrior in these words

explanation.surface: A man as brave as a lion and as surly as a bear, so Alexander thinks.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's 'Troilus and Cressida' (1.2), Alexander describes the Greek champion as 'valiant as the lion, churlish as the bear'; 'Alexander' is not Alexander the Great.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's servant Alexander uses these words for the Greek warrior who fights Hector.

clue.text: Beethoven's lyricist

parts.note: the words of the choral finale of the Ninth Symphony, the Ode to Joy, are by a German poet

explanation.surface: The man who wrote words for Beethoven.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ninth Symphony's choral finale sets the poem 'An die Freude' (Ode to Joy).
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich Schiller wrote the poem 'An die Freude' that Beethoven set in his Ninth Symphony.

clue.text: Hard, but familiar, Irish name of last king of Israel

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
O'Shea is a well-known Irish surname

explanation.surface: A tough yet common Irish surname belonged to Israel's final ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoshea was the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, conquered by Assyria (2 Kings 17).
explanation.definitionFit: Hoshea reigned over the northern kingdom until its fall to Assyria around 722 BC.

clue.text: Philosopher recognized in wrecked shop annexe

indicators.note: a wrecked building is ruined and broken apart, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A thinker is spotted in the ruins of an outbuilding beside a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of SHOP ANNEXE are rearranged to name the Greek thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenophanes of Colophon was a pre-Socratic Greek poet-thinker who mocked anthropomorphic gods.
